name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,879

clue.text: Sergeant major really in favour of cough sweet gets mint

blocks.note: SM is the army's shorthand for the rank, the two initials on a duty roster
somebody really in favour of a plan is all for it, six letters that arrive as one phrase
Tunes were a British brand of menthol lozenge, sold in a roll for a blocked nose

explanation.walkthrough: The surface keeps you in the sweetshop right to the last word, and that last word is the definition: not the herb or the confectionery but the money sense.
explanation.definitionFit: mint -> SMALL FORTUNE: both are idioms for a very large sum of money, and 'small' in the answer is pure irony.

clue.text: Without good weather one's upset

indicators.note: Something upset has been tipped right over, and in a down entry that means reading the assembled letters from the bottom of the grid upwards.

blocks.note: fine weather comes from the sun, three letters laid down first
'one' in the formal sense is the speaker, so 'one's' is written I'm before anything is turned

explanation.walkthrough: It is the whole stack that turns, not each piece on its own: build the two bits in clue order, then read the five letters back up the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Without -> MINUS: both mean lacking something, and 'a week minus the weekend' says exactly what 'a week without it' says.

clue.text: Untidy business spotted in toilet, diapers emptied out?

indicators.note: One thing placed in another goes bodily inside it, so this word is what splits the letters already gathered.
A container emptied out keeps only its walls, so the word beside it gives up everything between its first and last letters.

blocks.note: the everyday British word for one, and it opens up to take a guest
whatever was spotted was seen, and this is what drops into the gap
the outside letters survive and the five in the middle are thrown away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Business' is not trade here but the vaguer sense of a matter or affair. 'Diapers' is the American word, which is why nothing British-sounding is being emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: Untidy business -> LOOSE ENDS: the phrase names the details of a job left dangling, which is business at its untidiest.

clue.text: Thin metal ship has cracked, being rock-bound

indicators.note: Something cracked has split open, and the letters in front of the phrase part company to let the next piece into the gap.

blocks.note: kitchen foil is metal rolled thin, and it splits after its second letter
SS is the prefix on a steamship's name, and it drops into the split

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a vessel in trouble; underneath, the vessel is two letters and the trouble is what lets them in. 'Being' is a creature, not the participle it looks like.
explanation.definitionFit: being rock-bound -> FOSSIL: the remains of a creature turned to stone and locked in rock, so 'being' is the noun, a living thing.

clue.text: Change advocate dealing with ex

blocks.note: RE heads a memo to say what it deals with, the standard two letters for 'concerning'
an ex-anything is a former one, plain synonym

explanation.walkthrough: The tempting split is 'Change' on its own, leaving 'advocate' to supply letters. Both words are the definition together, and the wordplay is only the last three.
explanation.definitionFit: Change advocate -> REFORMER: a reformer campaigns for an institution to be changed rather than swept away, so arguing for change is the whole job.

clue.text: Perfect golf club short of parking

indicators.note: To be short of a thing is to be missing it, so the word beside the phrase turns up without the letter named after it.

blocks.note: the club a golfer takes out on the green, six letters before anything goes
P is the letter on a British road sign for parking, and this is the one that leaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect' is not the verb but the intensifier, the sense in 'a perfect fool' - which is why an adjective meaning complete is what answers it.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect -> UTTER: both are intensifiers meaning absolute, so a perfect stranger and an utter stranger are the same person.

clue.text: April ice melting around start of month, going by experience

indicators.note: What melts around a thing closes over it, so the single letter named next finishes up buried among the rest.
The start of a word is the letter it begins with, and that one letter is all this asks for.

blocks.note: eight letters of raw material: the month and the frozen water are there to be dissolved, not read
the first letter of the word that follows, joining the pool

explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' tempts you to build a container, with something wrapped round an M. The melting has already dissolved everything, so the M is simply one letter of the nine.
explanation.definitionFit: going by experience -> EMPIRICAL: empirical knowledge is what observation and trial produce, as opposed to what theory predicts.

clue.text: Short of cash, after a single drink for each son

blocks.note: 'on arrival' means after arriving, so 'on' is one of the words English uses for after
a single of anything is one of it
to sup is to drink, the old verb that survives in 'supping ale'
per is Latin for each, as in miles per hour
S is the standard family-tree abbreviation for son

explanation.walkthrough: The joins never fall where the wordplay does: the S that closes the second word is the front of the drink, and the son's S is the very last letter of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Short of cash -> ON ONE'S UPPERS: the idiom pictures shoes worn through the soles until only the uppers are left, so the wearer is broke.

clue.text: Dog performing with duck coming last?

indicators.note: Whatever comes last ends up at the back, so the bird's letter leaves the place it sits in and is written on the end instead.

blocks.note: to be performing is to be doing, and these four letters are what is left when the bird's is taken out
a batsman out for no runs has scored a duck, and no runs is written as a nought

explanation.walkthrough: 'Performing with duck' reads as a circus act. The duck is cricket's nought, and the question mark is there because the letter will not stay where its own word puts it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog -> DINGO: the wild dog of the Australian outback, so the definition names the family the animal belongs to.

clue.text: Two pegs Ronald fashioned in identical spirit

indicators.note: Something fashioned has been worked into a new shape, and the letters beside the word are worked into a new order.

blocks.note: the word is written out twice over, six letters of raw material rather than a description
the name goes into the mix whole, all six of its letters

explanation.walkthrough: Count before you shuffle. The fodder only reaches twelve letters if 'Two pegs' means the word spelled out twice, which is the step the surface hides.
explanation.definitionFit: identical spirit -> DOPPELGANGER: German for 'double-goer', the ghostly twin of a living person, so it is a spirit and an exact likeness at once.

clue.text: Fixing device you can't see the point of?

blocks.note: read straight: a small thing for holding two pieces of fabric together, the sort that lives in a sewing tin

blocks.clueFragment: you can't see the point of?
blocks.note: the surface says pointless; the setter means the sharp end really is out of sight, folded away under its little metal clasp

explanation.walkthrough: There are no letters to collect here. The clue is one joke told twice over: no point as futility, and a point genuinely hidden so that it cannot prick anybody.
explanation.definitionFit: Fixing device -> SAFETY PIN: it fastens two pieces of cloth to each other, which is fixing in the fastening sense rather than the mending one.

clue.text: Is trooper on manoeuvres bringing up the rear?

indicators.note: Troops on manoeuvres are marched about the field into fresh positions, and the nine letters beside the phrase take fresh positions too.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material: the soldier is not a soldier here, only a supply of letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is adjectival, not the polite noun for a backside. Whatever brings up the rear is the hindmost of its line, and that is the sense wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: bringing up the rear -> POSTERIOR: posterior means situated behind or coming after, so whoever is last in a column is the posterior one.

clue.text: Programme you might have seen about sport, endless one

indicators.note: A word made endless loses the letters at both of its ends, and with a three-letter word only the middle one is left standing.

blocks.note: RE is the shorthand at the head of a memo, meaning 'about'
RU is rugby union, one of the games a British crossword shortens to two letters
strip a letter off each end of the number and a single one survives

explanation.walkthrough: The tempting move is to dock the number at the tail and get ON. Endless means no ends at all, and only then do the pieces come to five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Programme you might have seen -> RERUN: a rerun is a repeat showing, so anyone watching may well have caught that episode before.

clue.text: Missouri town at the cinema, going out

blocks.note: the invented town of the 2017 film 'Three Billboards Outside ---, Missouri', so the place exists only on screen
said of the tide: the twice-daily retreat of the sea back down the beach

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing to take apart. The two senses have nothing to do with each other, and the comma is doing all the work of hiding the seam between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the fictional town of a well-known film, and a tide going out, which is what a tide is doing when it ebbs.

clue.text: Distribute beer to old Glaswegian drunk

indicators.note: To distribute things is to scatter them about, and the nine letters after the word are scattered into a new order.

blocks.note: nine letters of raw material, three ordinary words handed over for their spelling

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has somebody handing out drink and the wordplay hands out letters. 'Old' is fodder rather than the usual single O, which is what makes the count come right.
explanation.definitionFit: Glaswegian drunk -> BLOOTERED: Scots slang for thoroughly drunk, the word you would hear in Glasgow and nowhere south of it.

clue.text: Greens sanctioned peace agreements, putting Republican out

indicators.note: Putting somebody out is getting rid of them, so the letter that stands for the party is thrown out of the word in front.

blocks.note: to let a thing happen is to sanction it
a truce is an agreed pause in the fighting, and the plural is six letters long before anything goes
R is the standard abbreviation for a Republican in American politics, and this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a party-political headline and every word of it is doing a second job: the sanction is permission, the peace deals are a plural noun, and the party is one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Greens -> LETTUCES: 'greens' is the everyday word for leaves eaten as vegetables, and these are the commonest of the salad ones.

clue.text: PM thanks Tories regularly, every single one

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval.

blocks.note: ta is the everyday British way of saying thanks
the second, fourth and sixth letters of the party, taken in order
every single one of a group is each of them

explanation.walkthrough: Irish politics, not British: the Tories in the clue and the prime minister in the definition sit in different parliaments, which is the joke and the trap in one.
explanation.definitionFit: PM -> TAOISEACH: the head of the Irish government holds this title, so the definition points at the equivalent office rather than translating the word.

clue.text: Tree by the beach still sheltering old policeman

indicators.note: To shelter people is to take them in, so the word in front opens up and holds the two pieces named after it.

blocks.note: still water is calm, and these four letters part company after the first
O is the usual single letter for old
a cop is a policeman, informally

explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' is the tempting word. It wants to mean 'even now', and the wordplay needs the quiet sense, water without a ripple on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tree by the beach -> COCO PALM: the coconut palm is the tree that lines tropical shores, so a beach is exactly where you would find one.

clue.text: Congratulations are expected at event, according to Spooner

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for trading the opening sounds of two words, so naming him is the whole instruction.

blocks.note: if you are expected somewhere then you should be there; this word gives its opening SH away and takes a G
to be at an event is to go to it, and this word collects the SH that its neighbour dropped

explanation.walkthrough: Say the plain version first - somebody expected at an event should go - then trade the openings. What comes out is British praise, as dated as the reverend himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Congratulations -> GOOD SHOW: an old-fashioned British exclamation of approval, said to someone who has done well, doing the job of 'well done'.

clue.text: Come and see this smoke

blocks.note: the fairground barker's shout, two words hollered outside a tent to pull a crowd in
the noun: a cigarette somebody has made for themselves out of loose tobacco and a paper

explanation.walkthrough: Five words and no wordplay at all. The shout and the cigarette have nothing in common, and 'this' is the nudge saying the second half is a thing rather than an action.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: 'Roll up!' is the showman's cry inviting people to come and see, and a roll-up is a hand-rolled cigarette.

clue.text: Travelling salesman set up rural department stores

indicators.note: In a down entry, letters set up are read from the bottom towards the top, so they come out the other way round.
To store a thing is to keep it inside, so the two words beside this one are holding a run of letters between them.

blocks.note: six letters in a row straddle the space between the two words, sitting there back to front

explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface belongs to retail, which is the disguise: the shop talk hides a run of letters that has to be read the wrong way along the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling salesman -> PEDLAR: a pedlar carries goods from door to door on foot, which is selling on the move in its oldest form.

clue.text: Roger rather than Edward

blocks.note: choosing one thing rather than another is choosing it and not the other
Ed is the everyday short form of the name

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is hunting for a man. 'Roger' is not a person here but radio-speak for 'understood', and it is the word doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger -> NOTED: radio operators say Roger to confirm a message has been received and understood, which is what noting it means.

clue.text: Homeric quote you cut short in ring with heavyweights

indicators.note: A word cut short stops before it was due to end, so the pronoun beside the phrase arrives two letters long.

blocks.note: the Homer wanted is Homer Simpson, and his groan of self-reproach is his whole contribution
the pronoun gives up its final letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Homeric' points at the Iliad and means the cartoon. Once you accept Springfield rather than Greece, the quote is a single syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: ring with heavyweights -> DOHYO: the raised clay circle a sumo bout is fought in, and sumo wrestlers are the heaviest athletes in sport.

clue.text: Exaggerate love with poem full of rubbish

indicators.note: Something full of a thing has it inside, so the letters in front open up and take what follows into the middle.

blocks.note: in tennis a score of nothing is called love, and nothing is written as a nought
a poem is verse, and these five letters part company before the last of them
tat is cheap and shoddy stuff, the goods on a bad market stall

explanation.walkthrough: A love poem full of rubbish is a complete picture, and that is what makes the seams hard to find: three separate pieces, and the middle one has to split.
explanation.definitionFit: Exaggerate -> OVERSTATE: to overstate a case is to put it more strongly than the facts warrant, which is what exaggerating does.

clue.text: Strange story that article covers

indicators.note: To cover a thing is to lie over the top of it, so the two letters named here close around what they are covering.

blocks.note: one of English's three articles, and it opens up between its two letters
a story in the sense a child is told off for telling, an untruth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange story' reads as one phrase and the definition is only the first word of it. The story is the fib sense, which is the step most solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange -> ALIEN: what is alien is foreign to everything you know, so it strikes you as strange rather than merely unfamiliar.

clue.text: Father lost everything in landslide

indicators.note: Somebody lost has wandered out of position, and the letters beside the word wander out of theirs.

blocks.note: six letters handed over as material rather than read as a person
everything is all of it, three more letters for the pile

explanation.walkthrough: Read as English it is a man ruined at the tables. Read as instructions it is nine letters and a signal to rearrange them, and the signal is one small word.
explanation.definitionFit: landslide -> EARTHFALL: the name says what it is, a mass of earth dropping down a slope, which is what a landslide amounts to.

clue.text: Fake ID unfortunately getting one imprisoned

indicators.note: A prisoner is shut inside walls, so the single letter named beside the word is locked into the middle of the four around it.

blocks.note: alas is the old-fashioned word for unfortunately, and it splits after its second letter
the Roman numeral for one is a single upright stroke

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fake ID unfortunately' reads as one rueful phrase. The definition stops after two words, and the sigh that follows is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Fake ID -> ALIAS: an alias is the false name somebody goes by, the identity they hand over instead of their own.

clue.text: Date weird chat room men? I say it'll end badly

definitions.note: The definition is voiced by the answer itself: instead of describing the person from outside, the setter lets them announce themselves in the first person.

indicators.note: Something weird is not as it ought to be, and the letters beside the word are not in the order they ought to be either.

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for date, and it joins the letters being shuffled
eleven letters of raw material, there for their spelling and not their meaning

explanation.walkthrough: The surface tells a small sad story about internet dating. Even the first word is fodder, which is why the shuffle needs twelve letters where the phrase supplies eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: I say it'll end badly -> DOOM-MERCHANT: a doom merchant deals in gloomy predictions, forever announcing that whatever it is will turn out badly.
